video.title: Fitting a line: A model that predicts
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor - the students' science teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our class kept a reading diary for a term. Students who read more often scored higher in the reading test. Could we predict a new student's mark from their reading hours?
Today: how a straight line can predict, and when not to trust it.

scenes.on_screen_text: A model: a simple rule that predicts
scenes.narration: A model is a simple rule learned from data that makes a prediction. The simplest model is a straight line through a scatter plot. Finding that line is called linear regression.
Many lines could pass through the dots. The best fit line keeps the gaps between the dots and the line as small as possible. The computer finds it in a moment.
Here are average marks for pupils grouped by hours of reading each week. They climb steadily, about two marks for every extra hour.
The line has a slope and a start. Here the slope is two marks per hour, and the start is eight marks for no reading. So the prediction is eight plus two times the hours.
Careful with lines. Our pupils read between zero and five hours, so the line only knows that range. And a line shows a pattern, not a promise for one pupil.
Quick check! The slope is two marks per hour. If a pupil reads three more hours a week, how many more marks does the line predict?
Six more marks. Three hours times two marks per hour is six. That is what slope means: the change for each extra unit.
In the app, open the scatter lab and show the line of best fit. Drag one pupil far from the others and watch the line tilt.
Your turn. Our pupils read up to five hours. Should we trust the line to predict the mark for forty hours a week?
No, forty hours is far outside our data. Remember: the best fit line is a model, its slope is the change per unit, and it only works inside the data you had.
Try it yourself: measure the height and arm span of a few people, and lay a ruler where the line fits best. Predict someone new, then measure and compare.

checkpoints.prompt: The slope is 2 marks per hour. If a pupil reads 3 more hours, how many more marks does the line predict?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the slope is the change for each hour, so multiply 3 by 2.

checkpoints.prompt: Our pupils read 0 to 5 hours. Should we trust the line for 40 hours a week?

options.text: No, it is far outside the data

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a line only knows the range of data it learned from.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: outside the data we have no evidence the pattern holds.
